profile.subject: Elizabeth I of England
profile.overview: Elizabeth I inherited the English throne from her half-sister Mary and restored the Protestant Church of England. During her reign, a rival queen was executed and the English navy beat back a Spanish invasion fleet. Elizabeth never married, and when she died in 1603 the English crown passed to James VI of Scotland.

key_moments.title: Elizabeth takes the throne
key_moments.text: Elizabeth was at **Hatfield House** when word came that her half-sister **Mary I** had died. Soon afterward she made **William Cecil** her principal secretary. She asked him to give her the advice he thought best, even when it went against her own wishes.

key_moments.title: A new settlement for the Church
key_moments.text: With the **Act of Uniformity**, Parliament reversed Mary I’s repeal of an earlier prayer book and restored it with revisions. Ministers had to follow the **Book of Common Prayer** in public worship. A minister convicted of refusing to use it could go to prison.

key_moments.title: Mary, Queen of Scots, is executed
key_moments.text: While investigating the **Babington Plot** to kill Elizabeth, her advisers came to believe that Mary Stuart was involved. Elizabeth signed Mary’s death warrant, and the **Privy Council** sent it to be carried out at **Fotheringhay Castle**. After the execution, Elizabeth said she had given no instruction to carry it out.

key_moments.title: England turns back the Armada
key_moments.text: Elizabeth visited her troops at **Tilbury** during the invasion crisis. English ships fought **Philip II’s Armada**, and bad weather battered the Spanish fleet. In a letter to the queen, **Francis Drake** described the repairs the Spanish ships needed, down to their sails, ropes and masts.

deep_facts.text: At Windsor in 1593, Elizabeth translated **Boethius’s The Consolation of Philosophy** into English. Her secretary Thomas Windebank took down prose from her dictation. The surviving draft still has verse in the queen’s own handwriting, including a passage in which Orpheus’s song leaves a hare unafraid of a dog.

connections.name: Mary I
connections.connection: Elizabeth succeeded her half-sister Mary I in 1558 and restored Protestant worship.

connections.name: Mary, Queen of Scots
connections.connection: Elizabeth signed the execution warrant for her cousin, a rival claimant to the English throne.

connections.name: Philip II of Spain
connections.connection: His Armada failed to invade Elizabeth’s kingdom in 1588.

connections.name: James VI and I
connections.connection: Already king of Scotland, he succeeded Elizabeth as James I of England.

connections.name: Francis Drake
connections.connection: He wrote to Elizabeth about the condition of the Spanish fleet as it retreated in 1588.

issues: key_moments.1.text: “Mary I’s repeal” loosely ascribes the earlier repeal to the monarch. The cited 1559 statute says Parliament repealed it in Mary’s first regnal year. “Parliament restored the earlier prayer book, with revisions, after its repeal under Mary I” keeps the supported agency.

key_moments.1.text: “could go to prison” can suggest discretion at sentencing. The statute prescribed imprisonment upon lawful conviction for refusing the required prayers, including six months for a first offence. Describe the penalty as one prescribed by the Act.

key_moments.2.text / key_moments.2.source: “her advisers came to believe” extends to the group a conclusion the supplied account specifically assigns to Walsingham, and the lead sentence under 1587 can make the earlier investigation sound contemporaneous with the execution. Say that during the Babington Plot investigation of 1585–86, Walsingham believed he had found evidence implicating Mary in a plan to kill Elizabeth. Alford supplies this evidence. The displayed warrant acquisition notice supports the warrant, dispatch, venue and Elizabeth’s later denial, but does not support the Babington Plot sentence. Add Alford as a reader-facing source for that sentence if the format permits, or remove the sentence to stay with the warrant source.

key_moments.3.text / key_moments.3.source: The displayed Drake letter and accompanying text support the naval encounter, weather and damage report. The Tilbury visit is supported by the separate Folger catalogue, where Sharpe is identified as present. Starting with Tilbury also obscures the sequence: the report is dated 8 August and the catalogue dates the Tilbury speech to 9 August. If retaining the visit, put it after the letter and provide a reader-facing citation to its own evidence. Otherwise keep the moment focused on the encounter and Drake’s report.
